rationale:
CROSS-FILE `overrides` for cpp — the half of the label that had no CHANNEL, which is a different defect from having no pin.

`analyze()` declared three parameters, so the engine's fourth (`AnalyzeContext.overrideCompanion`) never reached this analyzer at all, and the resolver read `classBases`, a per-file map. `override-context.ts` names this exact failure for python: 'Python's `analyze()` had stopped at three parameters, so the engine's fourth never reached it ... The rule was written, wired to a channel, shipped, and had never run.' cpp's case was one step quieter, because no rule had been written yet, so nothing turned red — the kind of absence no gate reports. Measured cost of the per-file-only answer: 735 `override`-keyword sites in the corpus against 185 `overrides` edges emitted; the keyword is the author's own assertion and it was read for the `decorators` payload only.

WHY THE COMPANION IS NOT TRUSTED ALONE. It carries owner -> declared METHOD NAMES and no signatures, and a name alone cannot tell an override from C++ NAME HIDING — which is the confusion the M37.9 differential round recorded when it excluded cpp overrides from the oracle ('same-name across a base chain conflates C++ NAME-HIDING with virtual override ... different arity hides, it does not override'). PERL-MR15 measured 75.6% of its companion-only edges FALSE and withdrew them. So the two are combined: the companion proves the base DECLARES the method, the `override`/`final` keyword proves the method OVERRIDES one. Confidence is 0.95 rather than 1.0 because 'the first ancestor in declaration order that declares the method' is still a choice; the machine-readable `reasonCode` records which pair of facts established it, per M14-HONESTY-CONTRACT §4.

`ExternalDerived::probe` IS THE ROW THAT MATTERS MOST, and it is a RECALL LOSS rather than a suppressed falsehood — which is the distinction the whole design turns on. `ExternalInterface::probe` is `virtual void probe(int)` and the redeclaration matches it exactly, so in real C++ this IS an override; the analyzer does not publish the edge, because the evidence available across a file boundary (a NAME in the companion) cannot tell it from `tune` just below it, which is a name HIDE with a mismatched signature. Two candidate errors are available here — publish the hide as an override, or decline the override — and they are indistinguishable on this evidence. Declining is chosen because a false edge poisons bb_graph, bb_impact and bb_migrate in a way that a missing one does not, and because the population that IS provable (the keyword arm) is 735 corpus sites rather than the whole cross-file population. The cost is counted, not argued. `ExternalDerived::tune` is the same shape and is pinned the same way, so neither arm can move without the other.

A fix that widened the companion path until these rows moved would look like an improvement and be a regression: PERL-MR15 measured exactly that widening at 75.6% false.

The `LocalBase`/`LocalDerived` arm is the CONTROL: with the base visible in the same file the in-file signature check applies and the companion is irrelevant, so `act` gets the 1.0 `override-keyword+signature-match` edge and `hide` is refused. Without this arm a change that routed EVERY resolution through the companion would still pass the three cross-file rows and nothing would notice.

expectRelationships.note: the cross-file heritage edge, which is what makes an override resolvable at all.

THE POSITION. `ExternalInterface` is declared in a different compilation unit and is visible ONLY through the companion, so without `crossFileOverride` this file emits nothing for it. Two independent facts establish the edge: the keyword (the author asserts an override) and the companion (the base declares the method).
THE CONTROL, in-file base: the signature check applies, the companion is irrelevant, and with the keyword the edge is a FACT at 1.0 rather than a 0.9 inference.

forbidRelationships.note: THE ROW THAT MATTERS MOST, and a deliberate RECALL LOSS rather than a suppressed falsehood. `ExternalInterface::probe` is `virtual void probe(int)` and `ExternalDerived::probe(int)` matches it exactly, so in real C++ this IS an override — and no edge is published, because a name-only companion cannot tell it from the `tune` hide. This is the PERL-MR15 ruling applied rather than re-derived, and it is the row that would fail first if someone "closed the gap" by trusting names.

C++ NAME HIDING, cross-file: `ExternalInterface::tune(int)` and `ExternalDerived::tune(const char*)` are the same name and different signatures, so the derived one HIDES rather than overrides. `ExternalDerived` also declares no `override` keyword on it — writing one would not compile — so the companion's name-only entry cannot support an edge. Declining it costs nothing, because it is not an override; `probe` immediately below is where declining costs something, and both are pinned.
a base NOT in the local class's base list can never be the overrider, however the companion is consulted. `LocalDerived` inherits `LocalBase` only.

NOT EVEN PRESENT: `ExternalDerived` declares no method of that name, so there is nothing to override. A companion lookup that fired on the BASE's members rather than the DERIVED's would produce this edge.
